channel.title: Said & Checked: Energy — AskAmerica
channel.description: What officeholders said each day about Energy, and which statements government data supports, contradicts or rules out.

item.title: Said & Checked, Energy, 2026-11-20: none false or contradicted, 2 unsupported, 8 unsettled (Chuck Grassley, Shelley Moore Capito, Sheldon Whitehouse)
item.description:
No statement was found false or contradicted.

Unsupported and Unsettled

  • Chuck Grassley, U.S. Senator: “Currently, $16-8/10 billion in total value of Iowa projects--my home State--is stuck in the Federal permitting process.” Unsupported. No published estimate of $16.8 billion in Iowa projects awaiting federal permits was found; the search covered the warehouse catalog, web searches and Grassley's own remarks pages, which did not contain the figure.
  • Shelley Moore Capito, U.S. Senator: “Even the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times have endorsed the passage of this.” Unsupported. No Wall Street Journal or New York Times editorial on the bill was found; the search covered web searches for both papers' editorials, and their sites were not fetched directly.
  • Sheldon Whitehouse, U.S. Senator: “Reported as: Whitehouse also said the bill would make data centers pay for the power they use.” Unsettled. S. 5653 as introduced adds a Federal Power Act section 228 that bars shifting the incremental grid costs of data centers drawing 20 megawatts or more to other customers and requires recovery from the data center; it addresses grid costs they cause rather than power use in general. The Capito substitute that the Senate actually passed as H.R. 2347 on Nov. 19 could not be read, so whether the provision survived is unconfirmed.

item.title: Said & Checked, Energy, 2026-11-18: none false or contradicted, 3 unsettled (Bruce Westerman, Alan Armstrong)
item.description:
No statement was found false or contradicted.

Unsettled

  • Bruce Westerman, U.S. Representative from Arkansas: “The USGS has quadrupled the Nation's geophysical survey data coverage since its inception.” Unsettled. USGS's Earth MRI progress page reports magnetic-radiometric survey coverage of the U.S. rising from 7% before the program to 26% in FY2025, about 3.7 times the starting level. That is near, but on USGS's rounded figures just short of, quadrupling.
  • Alan Armstrong, U.S. Senator from Oklahoma: “requiring new facilities to pay 100 percent of all grid upgrade costs and pay the full tariff on the existing system, rather than receiving subsidized rates” Unsettled. The introduced text of S. 5653 adds Federal Power Act section 228, which bars allocating any 'incremental cost' of serving a data-center load of 20 megawatts or more to other customers. Incremental cost is defined to include generation, transmission and distribution costs, which matches the grid-upgrade part. No '100 percent' or 'full existing tariff' wording was found, and a provision letting states set different rates for covered loads was not fully read.
  • Alan Armstrong, U.S. Senator from Oklahoma: “the renewables industry, the fossil fuel industry, hydropower, geothermal, and mining all stuck together to support this legislation” Unsettled. Oil and gas companies' support is documented: API-compiled statements from ExxonMobil, bp, Chevron and others back the bill. No published positions were found for renewables, hydropower, geothermal or mining trade groups, so whether all of them backed it was not established.

4 statements by 3 officeholders. 4 checked: 1 supported, 3 unsettled · 0 not checkable.

item.title: Said & Checked, Energy, 2026-11-17: none false or contradicted, 8 unsettled (Ed Markey)
item.description:
No statement was found false or contradicted.

Unsettled

  • Ed Markey, U.S. Senator from Massachusetts: “There are 17 data centers getting proposed right now for construction on our public lands, covering more than 17,000 acres of public lands across six Western States.” Unsettled. A Pipeline & Gas Journal report of a Center for Western Priorities analysis of Bureau of Land Management records counts at least 17 proposed data center campuses on public lands in six western states (Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Wyoming), and more than 24,000 acres across all 35 data-center-related applications; acreage for the 17 campuses is not broken out, and the BLM records were not read directly.
  • Ed Markey, U.S. Senator from Massachusetts: “under this bill, any data center that is less than two acres gets considered under a general permit, not a site-specific permit.” Unsettled. The only two-acre provision found in the Senate substitute text covers Clean Water Act general permits for fill discharges into less than 2 acres of navigable waters, not a data center's site size; no provision tying data center size to a general permit was found, which leaves open a different text version or a legal reading.
  • Ed Markey, U.S. Senator from Massachusetts: “this bill would bring economywide emissions down by 3.8 percent by 2040 compared to business as usual.” Unsettled. Rhodium Group's modeling projects 2040 emissions about 4 percent below current policy in its low-emissions scenario, about 3 percent in its middle scenario and about 0 percent in its high scenario; no source read gives 3.8 percent, and the model covers only some of the bill's provisions.
